myth: The ozone hole can't be fixed.
fact: It is healing. NOAA and NASA ranked the 2025 Antarctic ozone hole the fifth smallest since 1992, when the Montreal Protocol began to take effect, and the ozone layer remains on track to recover fully later this century.
source_name: NOAA, 2025 ozone hole is 5th smallest since 1992

myth: If an asteroid were coming, there would be nothing we could do.
fact: Humanity has already moved one. NASA's DART spacecraft hit the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos in 2022 and shortened its orbit by 33 minutes and 15 seconds.
source_name: NASA, Asteroid's orbit, shape changed after DART impact

myth: Asteroid Apophis will hit Earth in 2029.
fact: It won't. Apophis will safely pass close to Earth on April 13, 2029, and NASA is confident there is no risk of it impacting our planet for at least 100 years.
source_name: NASA, Asteroid Apophis

myth: Asteroid 2024 YR4 is going to hit us in 2032.
fact: In early 2025 it briefly had a small chance of hitting Earth. More observations showed it poses no significant risk to Earth, and in 2026 NASA ruled out a Moon impact too.
source_name: NASA, observations eliminate chance of 2032 lunar impact

myth: Bleached coral is dead coral.
fact: NOAA says it plainly: when a coral bleaches, it is not dead. If the stress is not severe, corals have been known to recover.
source_name: NOAA, Is coral bleaching the same as coral death?

myth: Solar storms hit without any warning.
fact: NOAA's SOLAR-1 watches the Sun from about a million miles away and is a cornerstone of the U.S. space weather early warning system, delivering storm imagery to forecasters within 30 minutes of capture.
source_name: NOAA, SOLAR-1 enters new era of space weather monitoring

myth: Nobody is doing anything about space junk.
fact: Agencies are acting. ESA guided its Aeolus satellite down in 2023 in the first assisted reentry of its kind, and ESA's Zero Debris approach aims to sharply limit new debris from its missions by 2030.
source_name: ESA, Space Environment Report 2025

myth: You can see the Great Wall of China from space with your own eyes.
fact: NASA says the wall isn't visible from the Moon, and is difficult or impossible to see from Earth orbit without high-powered lenses.
source_name: NASA, Great Wall

myth: Wings lift because air over the top has to race to meet the air underneath at the back.
fact: NASA calls this "equal transit time" idea the most popular incorrect theory of lift. Air over the top of a lifting wing really moves much faster than that idea predicts.
source_name: NASA Glenn Research Center, Bernoulli and Newton

myth: Astronauts float because there's no gravity in space.
fact: At the space station's height, Earth's gravity is still about 90 percent as strong as on the ground. Astronauts float because they and their spacecraft are falling around Earth together.
source_name: NASA, What Is Microgravity?

myth: It's summer when Earth is closest to the Sun.
fact: Earth's tilted axis causes the seasons. In the Northern Hemisphere, winter actually comes when Earth is closest to the Sun.
source_name: NASA Space Place, What Causes the Seasons?

myth: Shooting stars are stars falling from the sky.
fact: NASA says "shooting stars" are meteors: bits of space rock that burn up as they enter Earth's atmosphere at high speed.
source_name: NASA, Meteors and Meteorites

myth: The Great Pacific Garbage Patch is a giant floating island of trash.
fact: NOAA says it isn't a solid island. Much of the debris is small pieces of floating plastic that are hard to see, spread out by wind and waves.
source_name: NOAA Ocean Service, What is the Great Pacific Garbage Patch?

myth: The ocean is blue because it reflects the sky.
fact: NOAA says the ocean is blue because water absorbs the red part of sunlight, leaving the blue part for us to see.
source_name: NOAA Ocean Service, Why is the ocean blue?

myth: The far side of the Moon is always dark.
fact: NASA says calling it the "dark side" is misleading. As the Moon orbits Earth, different parts are in sunlight or darkness at different times.
source_name: NASA, Earth's Moon: Facts

myth: Lightning never strikes the same place twice.
fact: NOAA's National Weather Service says lightning often strikes the same place again and again, especially tall, pointy, isolated objects. The Empire State Building is hit about 23 times a year.
source_name: NOAA National Weather Service, Lightning Myths and Facts

myth: If it isn't raining, lightning can't hit you.
fact: Lightning often strikes more than three miles (5 km) from the center of a storm, and "bolts from the blue" can strike 10 to 15 miles (16 to 24 km) away.
source_name: NOAA National Weather Service, Lightning Myths and Facts

myth: If plastic has the recycling arrows and a number on it, it can always be recycled.
fact: The U.S. EPA says a plastic resin code on a product does not guarantee it can be recycled where you live.
source_name: U.S. EPA, Frequent Questions on Recycling

myth: Almost all the oxygen we breathe comes from trees.
fact: NOAA says about half of Earth's oxygen comes from the ocean, mostly made by tiny drifting plankton.
source_name: NOAA Ocean Service, How much oxygen comes from the ocean?

myth: You can only see the northern lights near the North Pole.
fact: NOAA says auroras form in two ovals, around the north and south magnetic poles. During big geomagnetic storms they can be seen over most of the United States.
source_name: NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center, Aurora

myth: Scientists have already explored the whole ocean.
fact: NOAA says explorers have seen less than 0.001% of the deep-ocean floor, and as of April 2026 only 28.7% of the seafloor had been mapped in high detail.
source_name: NOAA Ocean Exploration, How much of the ocean has been explored?
